sentences.text: The holotype specimen, cataloged as KZV-001, consists of a scattered partial skeleton that includes the front of the skull, three back vertebrae, and parts of the hip bone.
One unique feature is the upper edge of the upper jaw bone, which curves inward rather than outward as seen in later tyrannosaurs.
The three preserved back vertebrae possess exceptionally tall bony projections on their tops.
Large, oval-shaped nostrils are present, a trait that links this animal to the Proceratosauridae family.
Although enough bone is missing to be sure, the animal likely had a large ridge on its nose similar to other members of its family.
This creature was the biggest theropod found in the Early Cretaceous fossils of the Jehol region, measuring between 7.5 and 10 meters long.
Its massive size challenges the old idea that early tyrannosauroids were small and only grew larger in advanced species like Tyrannosaurus.
The remains were found in the Jiufotang Formation of Liaoning, China, dating to the Early Cretaceous period.
The specific name honors the Kazuo district in Liaoning where the fossils were discovered.
In 2016, scientists updated the size estimates to a length of 7.5 meters and a weight of 1.2 tons.
Being one of the largest known early tyrannosauroids, this animal refuted the belief that these predators gradually increased in size from small ancestors to giant apex hunters.
Sinotyrannus belongs to the family Proceratosauridae.
While early descriptions hinted it might be the oldest tyrannosaur because of its large size, later studies placed it firmly within the proceratosaurid group.
A 2016 analysis suggested that Sinotyrannus is a close relative of Yutyrannus, while placing other genera outside the Proceratosauridae family.
This animal lived approximately 120 million years ago during the Aptian stage in what is now Asia.
Its time range spans from 121.4 to 113.2 million years ago, covering the Aptian stage.
It inhabited a wet landscape featuring lush forests and large lakes.
The environment was also prone to frequent volcanic activity.
Recent studies propose that Sinotyrannus, known from an adult, could be a mature version of the earlier genus Huaxiagnathus, which is only known from young specimens.
